courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a realistic data-governance change (e.g. 'add a required data-classification field to every new table before it ships') and write it up two ways: as a Waterfall-style requirements document with a fixed end-of-project delivery date, and as 3 Agile user stories in the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' format, each with its own acceptance criteria.
slots.deliverable: One short Waterfall-style requirements writeup and 3 Agile user stories (with acceptance criteria) for the same governance change, so you can compare the two approaches directly.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a 5-column Kanban board (Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, Done — on paper or a spreadsheet) and place the 3 user stories from the previous slot onto it, moving your top-priority story into To Do; then, for that top story, write down what each of the Dev, QA, UAT, and Production stages would need to confirm before a data-classification change could safely go live — including who in Production actually owns confirming it after release.
slots.deliverable: A populated 5-column Kanban board plus a written Dev/QA/UAT/Production checklist for the top-priority story.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the exact Git commands (clone, branch, commit, push) you'd run to make the data-classification change from Slot 1, plus a specific, non-vague commit message for it; then write a release note for the change following the lesson's format (what changed, why, any known limitation), and name which deployment strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling, or feature flag) you'd pick for rolling out a change to a production data catalog, with one sentence justifying the choice.
slots.deliverable: A Git command sequence with a real commit message, a written release note, and a justified deployment-strategy choice.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the Castlebridge Retail capstone end to end: write the 3 required user stories (revenue-by-region, revenue-by-category, automatic refresh) with acceptance criteria, build the 5-column Kanban board, write a short QA test plan including the zero-sales-region edge case, write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice, write specific release notes, and write up how you'd investigate and communicate about the simulated production incident where one region's numbers show zero.
slots.deliverable: The full capstone deliverable set: user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board, a QA test plan, a UAT sign-off, release notes, and a production-incident response writeup.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can explain and apply how real IT teams plan, build, test, and release software -- Agile vs. Waterfall, Scrum and Kanban, the Dev/QA/UAT/Production chain, Git, and CI/CD -- and has run one full project simulation end to end, the shared professional foundation every later course in this path builds on.
